{
  "frontend": {
    "needed": true,
    "prompt": "Implement UI and client request changes to support the new sort enum without changing existing filtering or pagination mechanics. Do not invent new API parameter names beyond the existing "sort" (the requirement already introduces a sort enum). Follow these steps:

1) UI: Add a stable sort control that exposes exactly two options to the user (labels may be localized):
   - created_at_desc (default, e.g. label "Newest")
   - title_asc (e.g. label "Title A→Z")
   The control must only allow these two values; the client must not generate or send any other sort strings.

2) Default selection: When the list view first loads, select created_at_desc if no sort is present in the current route/state.

3) Requests: Include the sort parameter on every server request that fetches the list (including paginated requests). Reuse the existing pagination request mechanism (do not invent new page/limit parameter names). When the user changes the sort selection, reset the pagination to the first page and fetch page 1 from the server with the selected sort value. Do NOT attempt to reorder items already fetched for the current page on the client side.

4) Caching / client-side storage: If you cache pages or responses, include the sort value in the cache key so cached responses are segregated by sort. Do not use cached data from a different sort value to render the current sort.

5) Error handling: The server will return HTTP 422 for invalid sort values. Because the UI only sends allowed values, 422 should be rare; still implement existing/global error handling to display the server error to the user in the standard way. Do not attempt to silently map unknown server errors to other sorts.

6) Tests / verification: Add automated/manual checks to ensure:
   - the client sends the sort param on all list fetches
   - when sort is changed the client requests page 1 from the server (no local reordering)
   - cached entries are keyed by sort
   - server 422 is surfaced via existing UI error handling

7) Non-functional constraints: Do not change or reimplement any filtering logic on the frontend. Do not perform any client-side sorting of the full dataset; all ordering must come from the backend."
  },
  "backend": {
    "needed": true,
    "prompt": "Implement server-side validation and ordering for the new sort enum and ensure sorting is applied before pagination. Preserve all existing filtering logic and pagination interfaces. Do not invent new API surfaces or change existing filter/pagination parameters.

1) Parameter handling and validation
   - Accept the existing request parameter named "sort". If the parameter is missing or empty, treat it as the default value created_at_desc.
   - Accept only these exact values: "created_at_desc", "title_asc". If the client supplies any other value, return HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity using the existing error response format.

2) Query ordering semantics (apply after filtering, before pagination)
   - Ensure all existing WHERE filters are applied unchanged first.
   - Map enum -> ordering expressions (tie-breaker must always be UUID string in standard lowercase form ascending):
     a) created_at_desc:
        - Primary: created_at in descending time order, with NULLs appearing last.
          Implementation note: express this in the datastore SQL/ORM as "created_at DESC NULLS LAST" where supported, or equivalently ORDER BY (created_at IS NULL) ASC, created_at DESC.
        - Secondary (tie-breaker): UUID as a lowercase string ascending. If UUID is stored in a non-string type, convert to its standard lowercase string representation for ordering (e.g., in SQL: lower(uuid::text) or an equivalent in your ORM).
        - Final ORDER BY (conceptual): ORDER BY (created_at IS NULL) ASC, created_at DESC, <uuid-string-lowercase> ASC

     b) title_asc:
        - Primary: title ordered by Unicode code point (Unicode code point ascending).
          Implementation note: Use your datastore's binary/Unicode-code-point collation (for example, in Postgres use a code-point/binary collation such as COLLATE "C" or a collation that guarantees Unicode-code-point ordering; in MySQL use utf8mb4_bin). If your datastore requires a function-based approach to achieve code-point ordering, use that. The key requirement is byte/code-point order, not locale-sensitive ordering.
        - Secondary (tie-breaker): UUID as a lowercase string ascending (same approach as above).
        - Final ORDER BY (conceptual): ORDER BY <title using code-point ordering> ASC, <uuid-string-lowercase> ASC

   - Do not assume any additional null ordering for title beyond your datastore default unless explicitly required; only created_at has the special nulls-last requirement.

3) Pagination
   - Apply paging (LIMIT/OFFSET or existing pagination mechanism) after the ORDER BY is applied. The sequence must be: apply filters -> apply ORDER BY per the selected enum -> then apply pagination.

4) API contract and docs
   - Document the allowed sort values and the default behavior: when omitted default is created_at_desc; invalid values yield 422.
   - Document the exact ordering semantics (created_at nulls last; title code-point ascending; tie-break by uuid lowercase ascending) in the API docs so frontend and tests can rely on deterministic ordering.

5) Tests
   - Add automated tests verifying:
     a) created_at_desc orders by created_at descending with nulls last and ties broken by uuid-lowercase ascending
     b) title_asc orders by Unicode code point ascending and ties broken by uuid-lowercase ascending
     c) when sort is omitted, created_at_desc is used
     d) invalid sort values produce HTTP 422 and preserve existing error format
     e) pagination is applied after ordering (e.g., fetch page 2 after ordering yields the server-side next set)
     f) filtering unaffected: existing filters combined with the new ordering produce expected results

6) Implementation notes & examples (translate to your stack/ORM):
   - SQL (conceptual examples):
     created_at_desc:
       SELECT ... FROM items
       WHERE <existing filters>
       ORDER BY (created_at IS NULL) ASC, created_at DESC, lower(uuid::text) ASC
       LIMIT <limit> OFFSET <offset>;

     title_asc (Postgres example using binary/code-point collation):
       SELECT ... FROM items
       WHERE <existing filters>
       ORDER BY title COLLATE "C" ASC, lower(uuid::text) ASC
       LIMIT <limit> OFFSET <offset>;

   - ORM: compose equivalent ORDER BY expressions provided by your ORM (explicitly request NULLS LAST semantics where supported and ensure collation or binary comparison is used for title ordering). Convert UUID to its canonical lowercase string form for the tie-breaker ordering.

7) Backwards-compatibility and safety
   - Do not change existing filtering code nor pagination request/response formats beyond adding documentation about the new sort parameter and validation.
   - Ensure the new ordering is deterministic so that paging is stable across requests (the uuid tie-breaker is required to guarantee deterministic ordering when primary key values are equal).

8) Monitoring and rollout
   - Add/increase test coverage before rollout. If your platform supports feature flags/gradual rollout, consider enabling validation and ordering in a controlled release.

Do not invent or change client-side pagination parameter names, filter semantics, or response error formats; reuse the existing mechanisms and formats for validation errors and paging."
  }
}
